item.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=Bayesian+epistemology+formal+models+of+group+consensus+vs+individual+evidence+weight&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Projecting the real through active inference: a unified model of reality construction from neuronal dynamics to social consensus <i>a neuroscientific framework for psychopathology</i>.\", \"abstract\": \"How does the brain transform a chaotic stream of sensory signals into a stable, shared experience of reality? This theoretical paper proposes that the brain does not passively receive the world, but actively projects it - it continuously generates predictions about sensory inputs and updates its internal model when predictions fail, a process formally described by the free energy principle and active inference. We argue that this process can be understood through an analogy with quantum decoherence - the collapse of multiple possibilities into a single actuality. By integrating insights from this analogy with active inference, we show how the brain resolves sensory uncertainty into a coherent projection of reality. A central question we address is whether projecting reality changes it. We argue that it does: a strong, coherent projection reduces uncertainty, while a weak or fragmented one amplifies prediction errors, and a distorted one - diverging from social consensus - leads to alternative realities that resist correction. This projection operates in discrete, rhythmic cycles governed by brain waves and is fine-tuned by neurochemicals that determine how much we \\\"trust\\\" our predictions versus new sensory data. The Default Mode Network - the brain's inner \\\"sea\\\" of self-awareness, memories, and context - acts as a central hub that integrates and updates these projections. Crucially, individual projections are stabilized into a shared, \\\"solid\\\" reality through social interaction, language, and culture - a process we call collective active inference. Within this framework, psychiatric disorders are understood as disorders of projection - distortions in how the brain generates and stabilizes its model of reality.
